zones.label: Column 1
zones.note: Lexical aid consulted after independent scan reading: Entry Words Data of Nippojisho, NINJAL, Hideyuki Ohshima and Taichi Aida, version 202510 (supplied page subset), CC BY 4.0. Used for entry identification, not as a substitute transcription. https://www2.ninjal.ac.jp/textdb_dataset/en/nipp/index.html ; https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/

lines.note: Takitsuzuke means continuing to kindle or burn; the gloss begins with burning in a row. The visible terminal mark divides fieira across the next line.

runs.text: ra, ou continuar com fogos por algũ eſpaço

lines.note: Completes fieira and explains maintaining fires over a certain extent or interval. The abbreviation in algũ remains unexpanded; this is a continuation, not another entry.

runs.text: Hum peixe de rio muito estimado que cõ-

lines.note: Tara is described here as a prized river fish. The following life-cycle claim belongs to this historical definition and should not be replaced by modern zoological information.
Completes cõmummente: the fish is said usually to go to the sea to die. Preserve that statement even though the familiar modern referent of tara invites a different description.
The second tara entry names a thorny tree, also tarano qi. The abbreviation q̃ is visibly separated from aruore; l introduces the alternative name.
Tarachime is the poetic word for mother. The damaged initial is T, not OCR r; preserve the printed synonym Faua without changing its internal u to the more expected f.
Tarachine is glossed as father and mother, with Voya supplying the Japanese explanation. The poetic label P is distinct from the synonym and the Portuguese definition.
Tarachiuo denotes a father, explained by Chichi and Pay. The historical final uo is not a typographical substitute for a modernized spelling.

Tarai is a wooden basin or tub. The vessel word is ſelha: its initial lacks the rightward crossbar visible in nearby italic f, so the second pass corrects OCR felha rather than retaining a different letter on lexical grounds alone.
Tarai is the verb of being sufficient or complete, here rendered being perfect in something. The principal parts carry carons; OCR Tafai confuses the clear r with f.

runs.text: ou estar a couſa perfeita, & ſem falta.

lines.note: The gloss continues with a thing being complete and lacking nothing. This explanatory sense connects the verb to the negative forms below.
Yorozzuno cotoni tarǒta fitogia describes a person accomplished in everything. The final Ho begins Homem on the following row without a supplied hyphen.
Mem completes Homem; the next example begins Iinbutno tarǒta, describing completeness or excellence of personal appearance. Keep the checked final t in Iinbut rather than expanding it.
Completes tarǒta fito gia and starts its translation: a person of good appearance. The gloss is aesthetic here, not a claim about moral character.

runs.text: de perfeita fermoſura. O negatiuo deste verbo.

lines.note: Perfect beauty completes the second example. O negatiuo deste verbo introduces the negative forms that follow; historical fermoſura remains unchanged.
Tarawanu and tarawazu are negatives meaning to be lacking. The scan supports faltar, not OCR ſaltar, which would wrongly change the meaning to jumping.
Tarameqi and darameqi are alternatives for producing a sound, with the dictionary supplying their verb endings. The water-drop comparison on the next line specifies the sound.

runs.text: como quãdo caem goteiras dagoa, ou choue, &c.

lines.note: The sound is likened to dripping water or rain. Preserve the contraction dagoa and the historical choue rather than adding a modern vowel or apostrophe.

runs.text: Palmeira braua em cujas folhas eſcreuẽ

lines.note: Taraju is described as a wild palm whose leaves serve for writing. The visible headword starts with T, correcting Faraju; the final abbreviation in eſcreuẽ is retained.
Os da India supplies the people who write on the palm leaves. This short line completes the preceding relative clause and has no independent headword.

runs.text: Modo, ou ſõ de goteiar, ou cair agoa.

lines.note: Tararito expresses the manner or sound of dripping water. The initial is T and the mark over the o of ſõ is a tilde, not the OCR grave accent.
Taratarato is an adverbial representation of dripping. Adu. and Vt belong to the italic grammatical apparatus; the Japanese example begins on the following line.
Mizzuga taratarato votçuru means water falls dripping. The scan supports votçuru, not votçuriu, and the full agoa at the edge rather than a divided ago-.
Dalto ſoando completes the Portuguese example: falling from above with a sound. The short line modifies the water's fall, not a new sense of the next verb.
This taraxi means to deceive or beguile. The initial gloss reads Enganar, not Enzanar; its meaning distinguishes this verb from the homographic pouring verb below.
Taraxi and taraxite are names for a deceiver or beguiler. The alternative marker belongs to the dictionary apparatus, and the final punctuation is visible beside embaidor.
The separate taraxi entry means to pour or shed. Nami- begins the first example's namida, tears, and the printed division must remain on this physical row.
Dauo completes namidauo taraſu, shedding tears or crying. The Portuguese lagri- likewise continues into mas below; neither divided word is a new headword.
After completing lagrimas, Yodareuo taraſu supplies the saliva example, glossed Babarſe. This illustrates dribbling or drooling rather than weeping.
Chiuo taraſu means shedding blood. The Portuguese ſangue identifies chi here as blood, not another Japanese homophone.

runs.text: Folhas de ola em que eſcreuem os da

lines.note: Tarayo names ola leaves used as writing material. The gloss refers back to the palm-leaf context of Taraju, without requiring a modern botanical identification.
India completes os da India, the people using those leaves for writing. The line belongs entirely to Tarayo's definition.
Tare asks who; Tarega maittaca asks who came. The visibly comma-punctuated l introduces the alternative question on the next line.
Tareca maitta is the alternate question, translated Quem veo? The final printed question mark replaces OCR ẽ; Tare na- begins the indefinite expression below.
Ritomo completes Tare naritomo, whoever it may be. Keep the physical word division and the source's older form rather than replacing it with modern dare.
Tare, taruru, tareta describes letting something down from above. The following examples develop the literal downward action and its figurative extensions.
Xôbenuo taruru is the urination example. The o-mark is an upward-pointing circumflex on reinspection; por ſi, not par ſi, completes the Portuguese expression.
Daibenuo taruru gives the parallel defecation example. Fazer camara is the historical Portuguese expression, with por ſi completed on the next row.
After completing the previous phrase, Yodareuo taruru means to drool. Su- starts sudare, the blinds in the next example; it is not part of Babarſe.
Dareuo completes Sudareuo taruru, lowering blinds. The Portuguese calls them eſteiras, mats, and the next line specifies their use at windows.
Das janelas completes the window-blind gloss. Tçuriuo taru- starts another application of the same verb, now to lowering fishing tackle.
The explanatory Japanese Tçuribaride iuouo tçuru identifies fishing with a hook. Iuo is the fish being caught; do not replace the source's historical fish word with a modern synonym.
Anzol completes the fishing gloss. Iifiuo taruru then means to extend mercy, introducing a figurative use; the initial Ii has consonantal value, not two separate vowels here.
Ricordia completes miſericordia. Xitauo taruru introduces putting the tongue out and down; the translation's lin- continues into the printed gue below, an anomalous ending retained from the scan.

Gue completes the printed lin-/gue. Second-pass enlargement shows an e with an open counter, not the expected a of lingua; preserve the anomaly. Cami- then begins the hair example after the description of letting the tongue hang downward.

runs.text: Rapar a cabeça dos mininos co-

lines.note: Uo completes Camiuo taruru, glossed as shaving children's heads. Retain the dictionary's explanation rather than substituting the modern literal sense of letting hair hang.

runs.text: mo custumão em Iapão do primeiro ate os tres

lines.note: The shaving practice is described as customary in Japan from the first through the third year. Annos at the top of column 2 completes this sentence across the column boundary.
Annos completes the age range from column 1. Camitareno iuaiuo ſuru introduces the celebration associated with a child's first head-shaving; Fa- begins Fazer.

runs.text: zer festa a primeira vez que rapão a cabeça

lines.note: Zer completes Fazer: making a celebration the first time the child's head is shaved. The printed a before primeira is retained without adding an accent.
Do minino finishes the first-shaving celebration gloss. Its continuation indentation is visible and is restored in the page structure.

runs.text: Faces cahidas, ou maçãas do rosto der-

lines.note: Tarefô denotes drooping cheeks. The circumflex in the headword is distinct from the nearby tilde in maçãas, and the latter's printed vowel sequence is preserved.
Rubadas completes derrubadas, describing cheeks hanging downward. This is an indented continuation of the face description, not an independent item.
Taremiſo is strained miso. Miſo occurs within the Portuguese gloss and is recorded separately for optional whole-word typeface review; the source's italic presentation is retained here.
Taremo is explained as everybody with affirmative verbs. The contrasting interpretation with negative verbs continues immediately below, so the apparent opposition is intentional.
With a negative verb, the same expression means nobody or none. This is the second half of the grammatical explanation, not an unrelated lexical meaning.
Taremuxiro denotes mats hung as a doorway screen. The scan reads dependuradas, correcting the vowel in dependaradas; guar- continues into guarda.
Da completes guarda: the hanging mats serve as protection or screening at the door. The line is visibly indented beneath the headword.
Tarenaritomo means whoever it may be. This independent entry repeats the expression already illustrated under Tare in column 1.

The gloss describes a hemp-cloth door hanging, identifying the entry as Tarenuno in the supplied NINJAL index. The r-position is severely abraded; retain the visible Ta enuno with a gap rather than silently supplying a secure letter. Guardaporta is continuous.
This tari is flowing or running, illustrated by blood and sweat. Correr and the closing &c. are visible; OCR Corter and &t. are not Portuguese variants to retain.

The next tari is the defective verb of sufficiency or completeness. Preserve the visibly single t in ata despite the preceding atta and the NINJAL normalization; defect. has f, and no hyphen follows couſa.
Cazuni tatta illustrates a number being complete or exact. The translation joins perfeita and juſta, and the printed tatta is not modernized to another past form.

runs.text: o numero perfeito. O ſeu negatiuo,

lines.note: The number gloss ends, and Taranu is explicitly introduced as the negative of this verb. Its roman type contrasts with the surrounding Portuguese explanation.
Taranu means to be short of something. Gojǔni taranu supplies an example of not yet reaching fifty, with the Portuguese A- beginning Ainda on the next row.
Completes Ainda não chega aos 50, not yet fifty. The next example begins being two short of twenty; the round final numeral is recorded as 0 rather than the OCR letter o.
Tçu completes futatçu, two: two are lacking to make twenty. Faltão has t rather than OCR i; the final A- begins Amarazu on the following row.
Amarazu tarazuxite totonoyeyo asks for an arrangement with neither surplus nor deficiency. Preserve the historical imperative and the physical A-/marazu division rather than rewriting the syntax.

runs.text: lhai de maneira que não ſobeje, nem falte. He

lines.note: Lhai completes aparelhai, prepare or arrange. The Portuguese repeats the instruction that nothing should be excessive or missing, then begins a usage qualification.

runs.text: ſentido particular neſte modo de falar.

lines.note: The dictionary calls this a particular meaning in this manner of speaking. The visible words are modo and falar, replacing OCR mode and falor.
Tariǒ concerns another person's revenues or lands, explained by Yoſonoriǒ. The Portuguese adjective reads alheas, agreeing with terras; the carons and abbreviated Rẽda are retained.
Tariqi is another's strength or aid, explicitly Tano chicara. Enlargement reveals the weak dot and foot at the first i-position, supporting Tariqi rather than Tarqi; alheas corrects OCR albeas.
De outro completes the explanation of strength belonging to another. It does not introduce a theological qualification beyond what the printed gloss itself states.
Tariǔ denotes another school or transmitted tradition. Nagare has a descending g, not OCR p; Bechino and tçutaye give Japanese explanations rather than words embedded in Portuguese.

The Portuguese lists another art, doctrine, or sect. Second-pass enlargement shows a narrow i between e and t in ſeita, correcting OCR ſeta; the definition's broad range should not be narrowed to religion alone.
Taru is a cask or barrel, rendered Piparite or barça. The unusual printed diminutive Piparite is retained rather than regularized from a modern Portuguese dictionary.
Tarume is the transitive act of loosening or making slack. The principal parts lead to tarumuru, the form used in the rope example below.
Tçunauo tarumuru means to loosen the rope. The object marker uo and the Portuguese corda make the transitive construction clear.
The figurative example is relaxing one's attention or resolve, equated with Yudan ſuru. The visible capital Y replaces OCR I in the divided Yu-; Per met. is printed separately here.
Dan completes Yudan ſuru, becoming careless or slack. The damaged final Portuguese word reads nalgũa, in some, and retains its visible tilde rather than the OCR noise nalhjia.
Obra completes the explanation of slackening in some work or task. This short continuation belongs to the figurative sense of Tarume.
Tarumi is the corresponding intransitive loosening or slackening. Afroxar has f, and the abbreviated Permet. ends with t; the long-u principal part remains as printed.
Cocoroga tarumu shifts to one's heart or attention becoming slack. The nominative ga distinguishes this from the earlier object-marked Cocorouo tarumuru.
Tibiarſe completes entibiarſe, to become lukewarm or lose ardour. It is the second Portuguese paraphrase of the preceding figurative example.
Tarumiga yuqu describes progressive slackening. The Portuguese infinitive is Ir, not OCR Ie; eſta- begins the description of a thing that had been taut.

runs.text: ua teſa. ¶ Item, permet. Se diz de couſa

lines.note: Va completes eſtaua teſa, had been taut. The paragraph then announces a figurative application, retaining the compact printed permet. rather than expanding its abbreviation.

runs.text: que hia com feruor, & ſe eſfriou, ou afroxou.

lines.note: The figurative object had been proceeding with ardour but cooled or slackened. The worn endings support eſfriou and afroxou, not eſfricu or afronou; the entry ends here, without a continuation hyphen.
Taruqi names rafters, rendered by the historical building term Aguieiros. The internal letter is i rather than the OCR j; no modernization of the Portuguese term is imposed.
Taruqi bana concerns the exposed front or ends of rafters. The gloss's final word is eſtão, not eſtũs, and its description continues below.
Com as pontas juntas describes the rafters with their ends together. This completes the architectural definition rather than beginning a separate construction term.

runs.text: Caixas que ſeruem pera ſe darem de

lines.note: Taruxen is defined as boxes used for gift-giving. The precise relationship to wine casks is supplied on the next row; the gloss does not itself call the boxes money.

runs.text: preſente em lugar de barças de vinho.

lines.note: The boxes are given in place of casks of wine. Preserve barças as the source's vessel term and avoid adding contents that the definition does not specify.
Taſacu means work done by another person. Iiſacu begins the contrasting example of one's own work; restore the line to the headword margin, not continuation indentation.

runs.text: Obra q̃ hum fez cõ ſuas mãos. Vide ſuo loco.

lines.note: Iiſacu is work someone made with his own hands, followed by a see-its-entry cross-reference. The abbreviations q̃ and cõ and the printed mãos remain unexpanded.

Taſai means another person's wife, explicitly Tano tçuma. The abraded m is supported by its surviving strokes and the wife gloss; remove the OCR's spurious internal space and restore headword-margin placement.
The bottom-right word is the catchword Taſo., confirmed by the first entry of f475. Its final o and full stop are visible; it is page furniture rather than another body entry.
